A B S T R A C T
In this work, the effects of Cr addition on microstructure, carbide formation and mechanical properties of
Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C-xCr (x = 0, 3, 6, 9) strips fabricated under a near-rapid solidification condition are inves
tigated. It is found that Cr addition makes as-cast strips present a nonlinear evolution on yield strength, i.e. firstly
reduces and then increases beyond that of Cr-free strip, and the total elongation of as-cast strips clearly decreases.
The evolution is related to precipitation reduction of κ-carbides. increased dislocation density. and formation of
Cr C instead of κ-carbides in 9Cr strip with Cr addition. Annealing at 550 <sup>◦</sup>C for 5 h enhances yield strengths of
all strips due to more carbide precipitations. An observed unusual phenomenon is that after annealing, Cr-free
strip shows lower total elongation than the as-cast strip, while all Cr-containing strips show higher total elon
gation due to reduction of dislocations. Formation of Cr C carbides at austenite grain boundaries is a reason for
the lowest ductility of as-cast and annealed strips containing 9 wt% Cr. Analysis in 0Cr and 6Cr strips indicates
that both slip bands and dislocations contribute to ductility of this austenitic low-density steel.

3. Experimental results
3.1. Microstructure and mechanical properties of as-cast strips
XRD results indicate that all the Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C-xCr strips are
composed of austenite (denoted as γ) and ferrite (denoted as
\delta ) ,
, and
austenite is the major matrix phase, as shown in Fig. 1. With an increase
in Cr content, the ferrite phase (110) diffraction (2θ = 44.1<sup>◦</sup>) intensity
increases, which means that addition of Cr promotes the formation of
ferrite phase. According to XRD results by JADE, the austenite lattice
constants are 3.70 Å, 3.56 Å, 3.56 Å and 3.55 Å for 0Cr, 3Cr, 6Cr, and
9Cr strips, respectively. The metallographic photos indicate that ferrite
uniformly distributes in the austenite matrix, as shown in Fig. 2. Ac
cording to a quantitative measurement by Gatan Digital Micrograph, the
ferrite fraction is 10.2 vol %, 11.4 vol%, 14.8 vol%, and 19.6 vol% for
0Cr, 3Cr, 6Cr, and 9Cr strips, respectively. Moreover, Cr addition
changes the shape of ferrite from rodlike to block like gradually. It is
found from Fig. 2 (a) that all ferrites are in the center of austenite grains,
which means that δ-ferrite first nucleated and grew from melt during the
near-rapid solidification. The experimental results agree with the so
lidification mode of this alloy: FA (ferrite-to-austenite) [2,4], i.e. L
(liquid) → L+δ (high temperature ferrite) → L+δ+γ (austenite) → δ+γ.

Fe–28Mn–9Al-1.2C-xCr strips. The results indicate that with an in
crease in Cr content, yield strength first decreases from 724 MPa to 617

greatly enhances strain hardening rate in the steady hardening stage,
and it gradually increases with higher Cr content, which the average

addition increases the ultimate tensile strength, though total elongation

Fig. 12(b) and (d) are TEM images of annealed 0Cr and 6Cr strips
after tensile fracture. After tensile fracture, average spacing of 0Cr strip
increases to ~190 nm, but that of 6Cr strip decreases to ~60 nm
compared with as-cast strips, which is also evidenced by increase in
elongation of 6Cr strip and decrease in elongation of 0Cr strip. It is an
interesting phenomenon that although annealing promotes precipitation
of the κ-carbides in 0Cr and 6Cr strips, which is confirmed by changing
their yield strength and TEM images, an opposite change occurs in
average spacing in annealed 0Cr and 6Cr strips. In the annealed 0Cr
strip, more κ-carbides are present with an average diameter of 14 nm
precipitate in austenite, as shown in Fig. 9, and thus these coarse car
bides are barriers for dislocations because dislocations can only pass
through those with diameter being smaller than 10 nm [32,45], while
the average diameter of κ-carbides is 8 nm in as-cast 0Cr strip.
Therefore, less slip bands are formed by shear mechanism during
stretching process, and total elongation significantly decreases. While in
annealed 6Cr strip, less κ-carbides are present with smaller diameter,
which can be easily passed through by dislocations. Thus, the precipi
tated κ-carbides of 6Cr strips after annealing slightly affect total elon
gation. Moreover, thermal stress and dislocations existed in as-cast 6Cr
strip partially disappear after annealing, allowing more slip bands to
generate during stretching process to increase its elongation.
A statistical measurement indicates that average widths of slip bands
in as-cast 0Cr and 6Cr strips are 13.4 nm and 12.5 nm, and the average
widths of slip bands in annealed 0Cr and 6Cr strips are 20.5 nm and 7.9
nm, respectively, after tensile fracture as shown in Fig. 12. These indi
cate that average width of slip bands is inversely correlated with spacing
between slip bands after tensile fracture. Finer slip bands and smaller
average spacing after tensile fracture are usually corresponding to high
ductility, and this phenomenon is termed as dynamic slip band refine
ment (DSBR) [35,43,46]. However, although κ-carbides in as-cast 6Cr
strip have the lowest content and the smallest size among three strips,
the total elongation after tensile fracture is lowest (as shown in Fig. 13)
due to its high dislocation density before stretching, which interferes the
relationship between slip bands and ductility. It can be concluded that
the dislocations play an important role in ductility of this austenitic
low-density steel, besides formation ability of slip bands during defor
mation process.
